Based on the data you provided, the short answer is: **Yes, you should be able to see the Moon quite easily.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on your specific conditions:

### 1. Altitude and Position
An altitude of **9.1 degrees** means the Moon is about 10 degrees above the horizon. While this is relatively low (it’s not "high" in the sky), it is well above the "atmospheric soup" of the immediate horizon where haze and ground-level obstructions usually hide objects. 

The azimuth of **109.26 degrees** places it in the East-Southeast. Since the Sun is currently at -16 degrees (well below the horizon), there is no direct solar glare to wash out the Moon's position.

### 2. Illumination and Phase
At **91.24% illumination**, the Moon is in its Waxing Gibbous phase (approaching a Full Moon). A moon this bright is one of the easiest objects in the night sky to spot. It will be significantly brighter than any star or planet.

### 3. Sky Conditions (Astronomical Twilight)
You mentioned the sky is in **astronomical twilight**. This is the period when the Sun is far enough below the horizon (usually more than 18 degrees) that the sky becomes very dark. Because the sky is clear and the Moon is nearly full, it will stand out with high contrast against the dark background.

### 4. Human Visibility
As an adult with normal unaided eyesight, your "limiting magnitude" (the dimmest star you can see) is usually around 6.0. A 91% illuminated Moon has a magnitude of roughly **-12.0**. This means the Moon is thousands of times brighter than the faintest star you can see. 

### Summary Verdict:
**You will definitely see it.** 

Because it is only 9 degrees up, you will need to look toward the **East-Southeast**. Since it is low, you may need to clear any nearby trees or buildings in your immediate line of sight, but as long as you have a clear "window" to the horizon, it will be very prominent.
